forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.40 sits 2.4% below Street consensus of $0.41, reflecting continued conviction that Wall Street is modestly overestimating Albertsons' margin resilience in what is historically the company's weakest quarter. While I'm raising my estimate by $0.01 from yesterday's $0.39, this acknowledges Q3's operating discipline (2.6% operating margin vs my prior 2.3% estimate) suggests cost management is marginally better than feared. However, Q4 faces distinct headwinds: SNAP benefit reductions affecting ~15% of the customer base, post-holiday promotional intensity, and competitive pressure from Walmart's price investments that management flagged on the Q3 call.

The key disagreement with consensus centers on buyback pace and underlying operating margins. Q3's blowout EPS beat ($0.55 vs estimates) was heavily driven by $750M in share repurchases that reduced the share count from 575M to 532M - a pace that cannot be sustained given $15.2B net debt (up from $13.9B a year ago). I'm modeling $200M in Q4 buybacks versus Q3's $750M, which provides a cleaner view of underlying earnings power. At 490M diluted shares and 2.0% operating margin (vs Q3's 2.6%), I derive $0.40 EPS. The Street appears to be extrapolating Q3's financial engineering into Q4 without adequately haircut for leverage constraints.

What would change my view: If management indicates buyback capacity remains robust despite elevated leverage, or if identical store sales come in above +2.5% suggesting SNAP impact is less severe than feared, I would raise my estimate toward consensus. Conversely, if gross margin shows any deterioration below 27%, the downside could be $0.35-0.37 EPS. Deutsche Bank's recent Hold rating with $18 target citing a 'mixed year' for food retailers validates my cautious margin stance.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2025 EPS estimate of -$0.07 remains substantially above the mechanically-derived Street consensus of -$0.17, reflecting my conviction that the consensus fundamentally misses the structural transformation in Adaptimmune's cost base. The -$0.17 consensus is backward-looking, averaging quarters that included the disastrous Q4 2024 (-$0.29 when R&D was $39M) and Q1 2025 (-$0.19 during heavy restructuring). The current run-rate operating expenses are dramatically lower: R&D has declined from $39M in Q4 2024 to $23M in Q2 2025 and I project $19M for Q4 2025; SG&A has normalized from $23M to $16M. This represents ~$27M in quarterly OpEx reduction, translating to roughly $0.10/share improvement versus year-ago levels.

The key supporting evidence is the costOfRevenue trajectory: Q1 2025 showed $879K, Q2 2025 showed $2.5M, indicating TECELRA manufacturing activity for 2-3 patient treatments per quarter. With TECELRA priced at approximately $2.5M per treatment and production lead times of 4-6 weeks, Q4 should see 3-4 treatments recognized at ~$8-10M product revenue plus $1-2M residual collaboration revenue. The balance sheet tells a concerning but separate story: with ~$26M cash at Q2 end and projected $18M quarterly burn, Q4 ending cash of ~$8M is critically low. However, dilutive financing is a Q1 2026 event, not a Q4 2025 P&L impact.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of TECELRA manufacturing/supply chain issues that delay patient treatments, (2) Unexpected restructuring charges or asset impairments, (3) costOfRevenue coming in below $2M suggesting commercial traction has stalled. The binary risk remains partnership/acquisition optionality - any strategic announcement could dramatically change the outlook, but I do not model unannounced events.

The company’s revenue has been demonstrably lumpy (e.g., $40.9M in Q3’24 versus $3.2M in Q4’24), and the 2025 run-rate through Q2’25 ($7.3M then $13.7M) supports a mid-teens-or-lower million quarter absent a discrete event. I therefore forecast $11.5M revenue, below the $20M proxy.

On earnings, the step-down in operating expenses from Q4’24 to Q2’25 is the key signal: Q2’25 operating expenses were $41.5M versus $76.7M in Q4’24. I model OpEx stabilizing around ~$43M in Q4’25, producing a net loss of ~$35.7M. With an assumed 290M WA shares (reflecting likely financing), that maps to EPS of -$0.123, which is less negative than the -$0.17 proxy.

I would change my mind if (1) there is evidence of a scheduled milestone/partner payment recognized in Q4’25, or (2) cash/liquidity actions imply materially higher dilution than modeled, which would push EPS closer to (or worse than) the proxy even if the dollar loss is similar.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2025 EPS estimate of $0.88 remains 17% below Wall Street consensus of $1.06, driven by my structural view that analysts continue to underappreciate AGI's interest expense burden and its compression of bottom-line profitability. The critical data point is the relentless upward trajectory of interest costs: from $16.3M in Q4 2024 to $18.7M in Q3 2025, I project $20.2M for Q4 2025 based on total debt of ~$990M at an estimated blended rate of 8.1%. This interest expense alone represents approximately $1.07 per share on an annualized basis, a massive drag that the Street appears to be underweighting.

The operational story is actually reasonably constructive - I expect revenue of $392M (+2.8% YoY), driven by seasonal Q4 strength in grain handling equipment and stable commercial segment execution. Operating income should reach $49.4M (12.6% margin), consistent with Q3 2025 performance. The disconnect between my estimate and consensus stems entirely from the below-the-line items: higher interest expense, modest other expenses, and a normalized 30% tax rate. The math simply doesn't support $1.06 EPS unless you assume either (a) materially lower interest expense than the debt structure implies, or (b) significant non-recurring gains.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of material debt refinancing at lower rates that I've missed, (2) Management guidance suggesting Q4 operating income significantly above $55M, or (3) A major one-time gain from asset sales or FX. Absent these, I have medium conviction that actual EPS will land in the $0.80-0.95 range, well below the $1.06 consensus. The news flow has been silent on AGI specifically - all available earnings call transcripts relate to unrelated tickers (AGCO, AJG, AGYS, GGG), providing no incremental information.

My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $1.15 remains approximately 5% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $1.21, primarily driven by the mechanical dilution impact that the Street continues to underweight. The Q2 equity offering of 3.5M shares was completed mid-quarter, meaning Q2's 37.0M diluted share count only reflected partial-period impact. Q3 will carry the full ~40.6M share count, representing a 9.7% sequential increase that suppresses EPS even as underlying net income grows strongly to approximately $38.5M - a healthy 11% sequential increase. The Street appears to be anchoring on the strong net income trajectory while insufficiently adjusting for the diluted share count mechanics.

The fundamental business remains exceptionally strong. AerCap's Q4 2025 commentary confirmed robust MRO demand and aging fleet dynamics that directly benefit AAR's aftermarket franchise. American Airlines' revenue growth projections for 2026, despite near-term government shutdown impacts, reinforce the structural tailwind from deferred aircraft retirements and maintenance needs. The Arkwin renewal validates competitive positioning in actuation systems, while declining short interest to 2.9% of float confirms the bear thesis is fading. However, the CFO transition adds approximately $2.5M in one-time costs that will modestly pressure SG&A.

My confidence level is medium-high because the dilution math is mechanical and highly predictable, while the underlying operating performance drivers - MRO capacity expansion, parts demand, and aftermarket pricing - all point to continued strength. What would change my view: (1) evidence the Street has already adjusted for full share count impact in consensus, (2) Oklahoma City utilization surprise above 75%, or (3) a buyback announcement that reduces the effective share count. Without these, I expect consensus to come down toward my estimate as we approach earnings.

My Q1 FY2026 forecast of -$0.04 EPS on $89M revenue represents a differentiated view from the published 'consensus' of $0.03 EPS, which I believe is a methodological artifact (simple 4-quarter average) that completely ignores BBCP's pronounced seasonality. The company has consistently posted losses in Q1 for multiple years - Q1 FY2025 showed -$0.06 EPS on $86.4M revenue, and Q1 FY2024 was similarly negative. Concrete pumping is a weather-dependent business that structurally underperforms in winter months when construction activity freezes (literally). Any analyst using a simple trailing average without seasonal adjustment is making a fundamental error.

My -$0.04 estimate is modestly optimistic versus Q1 FY2025's -$0.06 EPS, reflecting approximately 3% YoY revenue growth to $89M driven by IIJA infrastructure spending tailwinds. Management noted on the Q4 call that infrastructure investment continues to provide a positive offset to residential weakness. I'm projecting gross margin compression to 36.1% (vs Q4's 39.8%) due to lower equipment utilization - this is consistent with historical Q1 patterns. The $8.4M quarterly interest expense burden means the company needs roughly $8M+ in operating income just to break even pre-tax, which is difficult to achieve on Q1's seasonally depressed revenue.

I would reconsider my thesis if: (1) the company reported any Q1-specific operational updates showing materially better-than-expected activity levels, (2) weather patterns proved unusually favorable for January-February construction, or (3) management provided explicit Q1 guidance deviating from historical seasonal patterns. None of these have occurred. My conviction is high that the Street consensus is fundamentally wrong due to methodological error, not because I have superior insight into operations.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.97 represents a 3.7% premium to the Street consensus of $1.90, driven by continued operating leverage execution that analysts are underestimating despite four consecutive quarters of 5%+ beats. BNY's transformation under Robin Vince has fundamentally improved the earnings power of this franchise - the 507 basis points of operating leverage delivered in 2025 reflects structural efficiency gains from technology modernization and commercial excellence initiatives, not one-time factors. However, I am reducing my estimate modestly from $1.98 yesterday to account for Q1's typical seasonal headwinds: the annual compensation reset (merit increases, payroll taxes) typically adds $50-75M to expenses, while fee income seasonally declines 3-5% sequentially from Q4's elevated levels.

The key variant perception vs. consensus is that the Street continues to model BNY as a legacy custodian bank rather than recognizing the transformation to a higher-margin, technology-enabled financial infrastructure provider. Fee income now represents 75% of revenue, providing resilience and growth, while NII expansion from $1.16B in Q1 2025 to an expected $1.30B in Q1 2026 represents meaningful operating leverage. Management's track record of consistently beating consensus (average surprise of +7.3% over last four quarters) suggests systematic underestimation by analysts. The digital asset custody opportunity, highlighted at recent crypto conferences, represents upside optionality not fully reflected in estimates.

What could prove me wrong: (1) More aggressive Fed rate cuts than expected could pressure NII below $1.25B, (2) equity market weakness beyond current levels could impact AUM-linked fees, and (3) competitive pressure from fintech disruptors could accelerate more than expected. If Q1 expenses come in above $3.3B (vs. my $3.2B estimate), my EPS forecast would need to be revised down to closer to consensus.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.38 is 8.8% below the Street consensus of $2.61, reflecting continued skepticism about the pace of expense normalization and the sustainability of Q4's elevated net interest income. While Q4's adjusted EPS of $1.81 demonstrated underlying earnings power when stripping out one-time charges, the path to consensus requires both a strong seasonal trading quarter AND meaningful expense relief - a combination I view as unlikely given ongoing transformation investments. I'm modeling NII normalizing to $14.3B from Q4's $15.66B (which appeared to include one-time items), while trading revenues rebound seasonally to ~$5.0B from Q4's depressed levels.

The key disagreement with the Street centers on expense trajectory. Q4's SG&A surged to $13.84B from Q3's $9.96B, and while some of this reflects one-time restructuring charges, the underlying expense base remains elevated. I'm modeling $10.2B SG&A for Q1, which assumes meaningful normalization but not a full return to the sub-$8B run rate seen in mid-2025. This conservative stance reflects management's commentary about ongoing transformation investments and the likelihood of additional actions ahead of the May 7 Investor Day, which management described as outlining the 'next phase of the journey.'

What would make me raise my estimate: (1) Evidence that Q4's NII strength was sustainable rather than one-time, perhaps from favorable deposit repricing dynamics; (2) Clearer visibility on expense normalization timeline from management commentary; (3) Trading activity data suggesting Q1 client volumes exceeded typical seasonal patterns. Conversely, my estimate could prove too high if management front-loads restructuring charges ahead of Investor Day or if NII normalizes more sharply than I'm assuming. The insider selling by Cantu Ernesto Torres noted in recent news adds a modest bearish signal, though institutional accumulation by PNC provides some offset.

City Office REIT completed its go-private merger with MCME Carell (Elliott Investment Management and Morning Calm Management joint venture) on January 9, 2026 at $7.00 per share in cash. The company immediately filed Form 15 with the SEC to terminate its reporting obligations, making any public disclosure of Q4 2025 financial results highly unlikely. This fundamental reality renders this earnings forecast academic and essentially unverifiable - it exists solely for forecasting arena completeness.

My Q4 2025 estimate of -$0.12 EPS on $34.5M revenue reflects a continuation of the operating trends observed through Q3 2025, adjusted for the smaller asset base following dispositions and reduced interest expense from the substantial debt paydown executed in Q3 ($249.8M in net debt reduction). The revenue decline from $37.3M in Q3 to $34.5M reflects the portfolio shrinkage, while the improved EPS versus Q3's -$0.14 comes from lower interest expense and normalized depreciation (excluding Q2's $105M impairment-driven loss). These projections assume steady-state operations through the merger close with no material transaction-related distortions.

The key caveat is that this forecast cannot be validated. The acquiring consortium has no obligation to disclose financial performance, and the Form 15 filing confirms the company will not file a 10-K for Q4 2025. Any deviation from this forecast - whether from merger costs, asset impairments, or operational surprises - will remain unknown. My confidence level is low not due to analytical uncertainty but due to the impossibility of verification.

If the impairment were somehow deferred to closing day (Jan 9), I would be wrong, but ASC 360 'Held for Sale' criteria were almost certainly met in Q4 upon signing the definitive agreement.

IIJA funding is now flowing through to actual construction activity, providing a more durable demand backdrop than typical cyclical construction. CMC's $2B senior note issuance at favorable terms (5.70%/6.00%) signals management confidence in their pending acquisition and positions the company for continued consolidation. The stock's 69% appreciation over the past year and recent all-time high at $84.34 suggests institutional recognition of these structural tailwinds, as evidenced by Artemis's $104M stake.

My conviction remains medium given the mechanical nature of the tax/interest headwinds and the relatively predictable nature of CMC's construction-focused business.

Salesforce has demonstrated consistent operating margin expansion from 18.5% in Q4 FY25 to 21.3% in Q3 FY26, and I project this trajectory continues to ~24.3% in Q4 driven by restructuring benefits and scale efficiencies. I believe the Street may be over-extrapolating Data Cloud momentum or embedding overly aggressive Agentforce contribution. My segment build shows ~4.5% QoQ growth which is consistent with seasonal patterns but doesn't require heroic assumptions about AI monetization that hasn't yet materialized in reported numbers. The AcuityMD for Salesforce AppExchange announcement today validates the ecosystem expansion strategy but is immaterial to Q4 results. The ServiceNow cross-read from yesterday (21% subscription growth) supports enterprise cloud spending resilience, reinforcing my constructive stance.

My variant perception centers on margin quality over revenue quantity. The Street may be chasing headline revenue growth while underappreciating the margin expansion story. If I'm wrong, it will likely be because (1) large deal timing favored Q4 over my assumptions, driving upside to revenue, or (2) Agentforce is monetizing faster than public disclosures suggest. I'm maintaining medium-high conviction because the margin thesis has strong historical support, though Q4 seasonality introduces inherent timing risk.

What would make me change my mind: If Salesforce demonstrates material new customer wins or pricing power that offsets ServiceNow's competitive threat, or if deferred revenue conversion significantly exceeds historical patterns due to improved sales execution. Upside risk exists if Q4 seasonality is stronger than modeled, while downside risk intensifies if ServiceNow's growth accelerates further.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.46 remains 36% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.72, reflecting what I believe is a fundamental misunderstanding of airline seasonality and current cost pressures. Q1 is structurally Delta's weakest quarter - Q1 2025 produced only $0.37 EPS on $14.04B revenue - yet the Street's $0.72 estimate implies a near-doubling of profitability that is unrealistic given current fuel costs at $2.92/gallon (approximately $0.22 above Delta's January guidance assumptions, equating to ~$140M incremental cost) and labor inflation running at the high end of the 4-5% guided range.

The key disconnect is that analysts appear to be extrapolating the strong Q4 2025 performance ($1.86 EPS, +22% beat) into Q1 without adequately discounting for seasonal patterns. Q1 historically generates operating margins of 3-5% versus Q2's 12-14% peak season performance. Additionally, recent corporate travel indicators from other earnings calls suggest the recovery is stalling, which particularly impacts Delta's premium-heavy business mix. The JetBlue 10-K showing a $602M net loss for 2025 confirms the industry cost pressure environment hasn't abated.

What would change my view: If fuel prices decline materially below $2.70/gallon, I would revise upward. Similarly, if corporate travel demand shows unexpected strength in March booking data, or if Delta announces meaningful capacity cuts to protect yields, I would reconsider. However, absent these developments, I maintain high conviction that consensus is materially too optimistic and will need to revise downward as Q1 progresses.

Competitive capacity additions in premium routes

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.04 remains modestly above Street consensus of $0.03, driven by typical seasonal patterns that historically support sequential revenue improvement in Q2. The key to my above-consensus view is that Q2 typically benefits from enterprise budget cycle restarts and education segment timing, which should lift revenue from Q1's $64M to approximately $65.5M - a conservative 2.3% sequential improvement well within historical norms. While Q1's massive miss (-84% EPS surprise) spooked investors, much of that weakness stemmed from timing issues and accelerated expense recognition that should normalize in Q2.

The critical constraint on my optimism is the continued deterioration in deferred revenue, which I project to decline from $96M in Q1 to $88M in Q2. This leading indicator suggests weak new AAP bookings while existing contracts continue to recognize - a structural headwind that limits upside potential. SG&A remains stubbornly elevated at approximately $46.2M due to management's continued hiring expansion, which compresses operating leverage even with modest revenue growth. The Street's $0.03 consensus may be too pessimistic given seasonal tailwinds, but I'm not willing to forecast significant upside given these structural challenges.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) management's poor track record on execution - Q1's -84% surprise demonstrates unpredictability, (2) DOGE-related government contract uncertainty that could impact enterprise revenue, and (3) accelerating AAP attrition if economic conditions deteriorate. If deferred revenue falls faster than my $88M projection or SG&A exceeds $47M, I would revise down toward consensus. Conversely, if enterprise pipeline converts faster than expected, there's upside to $0.05-0.06 EPS.

I am projecting a significant beat vs. consensus (EPS 386.4 vs 304.8) rooted in a structural misunderstanding of Uniqlo's revised margin profile. Wall Street is currently modeling a sharp margin contraction (dropping to ~9.5% net margin from Q1's 14.3%), likely extrapolating historical seasonality and Chinese macro fears too aggressively. My analysis, supported by peer earnings from Ralph Lauren and Tapestry this week, indicates strong Western consumer appetite for apparel, allowing Uniqlo to maintain higher price integrity than modeled.

The 'Global One' pricing strategy has effectively decoupled Uniqlo's profitability from pure volume dependency, particularly in North America and Europe where the brand has transitioned from 'discount' to 'essential'. Revenue of 1.0T JPY is achievable given Q1 momentum, but the real alpha is in the Operating Income line, where I see ~155B JPY vs implied consensus of ~135B. 

I would revisit this thesis if intra-quarter data from Chinese peers (like Li Ning or Anta) showed catastrophic inventory builds, or if monthly sales data from Japan showed a sudden deceleration in Feb. However, current data suggests the consensus is stubbornly anchored to a bearish macro narrative that the company's operational improvements have outrun.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.85 remains 13% below Street consensus of $0.98, reflecting continued skepticism about the railcar demand cycle. The Street appears to be underestimating the severity of the manufacturing slowdown - Q1's 10.9% EPS miss was not a one-off but confirmation that the cyclical downturn has more room to run. I'm modeling revenue of $645M, down 8.6% QoQ, as railcar deliveries decline to ~3,100 units from implied ~3,300 in Q1. The backlog is depleting faster than new orders are coming in, and Class I railroad CapEx guidance has been consistently cautious. Gross margin compression continues to 14.0% from 14.6% in Q1 as manufacturing mix deteriorates.

I've modestly increased my estimate from $0.82 to $0.85 based on two factors: (1) working capital dynamics appear slightly more favorable as inventory drawdown accelerates, and (2) the leasing segment shows resilience with the $300M ABS issuance at 5.2% providing cost certainty. However, I'm still well below consensus because I believe the Street is anchoring on the strong Q3 2025 results ($1.86 EPS) rather than recognizing the structural demand weakness. The AlphaQuest 65.2% stake reduction is a meaningful signal - institutional investors are voting with their feet.

The key variant perception is that consensus appears to be modeling a V-shaped recovery in railcar demand that the underlying data doesn't support. New order rates remain weak, freight volumes are soft, and Class I railroads continue to emphasize cost discipline over fleet expansion. My bear case is $0.70 EPS if deliveries fall to 2,800 units; my bull case is $0.95 if management can surprise on pricing or mix. The ABS financing is a smart strategic move for long-term positioning, but it doesn't change the near-term earnings trajectory.

My thesis is anchored on the mechanical reality of Q1: a 90-day quarter creates a ~2.2% headwind to Net Interest Income (NII) that the Street estimates do not fully appreciate given the already compressing NII run-rate seen in Q4. I would revisit this bearish stance if deposit costs show a sudden, unexpected plateauing or if fee income shows a structural breakout above $55M. However, with recent insider selling and 'Risk Channel' news highlighting macro headwinds, the path of least resistance for earnings is lower. forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2025 EPS estimate of $2.88 represents a 27% premium to Street consensus of $2.26, reflecting continued conviction that Wall Street systematically undervalues JBS's multi-protein diversification during periods of segment-specific stress. The key variant perception is that analysts remain overly focused on the well-documented US beef margin compression (which Tyson's Q1 2026 results confirm at industry level) while underweighting the exceptional performance trajectory in poultry segments. Bunge's Q4 2025 results confirmed corn remains at multi-year lows, directly supporting Pilgrim's Pride and Seara's 12-14% EBITDA margin profile, which represents the primary earnings driver for Q4.

I've modestly lowered my estimate from $2.92 to $2.88 based on Tyson's Q1 2026 earnings call transcript which confirmed persistent beef margin headwinds are structural rather than transitory. However, the magnitude of adjustment is small because JBS's beef exposure is proportionally lower than Tyson's, and the offset from poultry strength remains intact. The 3.1% same-store sales growth from Restaurant Brands International suggests QSR demand remains supportive despite Chipotle's flat guidance concerns. The BRL at 5.7 (versus ~5.0 year-ago) provides meaningful translation tailwind for Brazil operations.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of material feed cost inflation in Bunge/ADM results that would compress poultry margins, (2) BRL appreciation toward 5.0 eliminating the export competitiveness advantage, (3) China export restrictions on Brazilian beef. The Q4 holiday seasonality provides a relatively predictable demand backdrop, supporting 72% confidence in this estimate versus a more uncertain macro environment.

Additionally, if management indicates on the Q4 call that the interest expense reduction is not sustainable or that operational momentum has stalled, I would revise downward. My conviction is high due to the clear Q3 call narrative and hard financial data on interest expense, but the thesis is contingent on stable macro demand and continued execution.

forecasts.thesis:
I am maintaining a High Conviction Bearish view against the consensus of R$2.26, forecasting R$1.71 instead. The Wall Street consensus appears to be extrapolating the Q3 earnings strength (which was aided by currency/hedging anomalies) while underappreciating the structural profitability crisis in the US Beef segment (~40% of revenue). Tyson's recent Q1 earnings serves as a critical leading indicator, confirming that the US cattle cycle contraction is severely compressing packer margins, a headwind that JBS cannot fully offset through its diversified poultry and pork divisions.

While the Poultry (Pilgrim's) and Pork segments are indeed benefiting from a favorable feed cost environment (corn/soy deflation confirmed by Bunge), the magnitude of the US Beef drag is mathematically overwhelming. My granular build assumes sustainable 8-10% margins in Poultry but barely breakeven to low-single-digit margins in US Beef. The consensus implicit margin profile requires a simultaneous recovery in Beef that defies the current biological cycle of US cattle herds.

I would revisit this bearish stance only if I saw concrete data indicating a sharp reversal in US cattle slaughter volumes (indicating better availability) or an unprecedented surge in international beef prices to China that could decouple revenue from domestic US costs. Currently, data supports the 'Tale of Two Proteins' narrative, where the bad (Beef) outweighs the good (Poultry) for the consolidated bottom line.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.68 remains 41% below the Wall Street consensus of $1.15, representing a high-conviction contrarian call grounded in Jefferies' demonstrably pronounced seasonal dynamics that the Street consistently misprices. The consensus appears to be extrapolating Q4's strong momentum ($0.85 EPS, $2.95B revenue) into Q1 without adequately accounting for structural Q1 headwinds: (1) elevated compensation accruals as annual bonus pools are established at fiscal year-start, pushing the comp ratio from Q4's 57% to an estimated 61%; (2) typical January deal completion delays that historically reduce IB revenue 10-15% sequentially; and (3) trading desk risk reduction post-year-end. Over the past five fiscal years, Q1 EPS has systematically ranged from 35-45% of the preceding Q4 EPS.

The Q4 2025 earnings miss (-8.6% surprise) provides critical validation of my thesis that Wall Street systematically over-estimates Jefferies' quarterly performance. Despite a strong fiscal year overall, the Street was caught offsides even on a Q4 that benefited from seasonal tailwinds. Peer earnings transcripts from Raymond James (Q1 2026) and Stifel (Q4 2025) confirm typical seasonal patterns without evidence of industry acceleration that would warrant an upward revision. Additionally, institutional selling patterns observed earlier this month (Thrivent -66.6%, Allianz -37.4%) suggest sophisticated investors share concerns about near-term performance.

I would reconsider my thesis if: (1) JEF pre-announced positive Q1 trading results or a major deal completion; (2) industry data showed atypical January M&A/IPO acceleration; or (3) management signaled a structural change in compensation timing. None of these conditions have materialized in 11 consecutive days of analysis. The $1.15 consensus implies a 135% Q1/Q4 EPS ratio vs. the historical 35-45% range - a fundamental mispricing that creates asymmetric downside risk for consensus holders.

The 4-quarter beat pattern suggests analysts are systematically underweighting MSC's ability to manage costs in a challenging demand environment.

Key upside would come from PMI surprising to the upside or customers restocking ahead of potential tariff increases. Downside risks include further manufacturing weakness or margin pressure from tariff-related cost increases. The DCF-based fair value of ~$77 versus current price of ~$84 suggests limited multiple expansion, but earnings execution should drive the stock from here.

My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains below consensus of $0.05, reflecting Richardson Electronics' fundamental cost structure problem that the Street appears to underappreciate. The company's SG&A has remained stubbornly fixed at $15.5-16M per quarter across a wide range of revenue outcomes ($51.9M to $54.6M over the past four quarters), demonstrating zero operating leverage. With Q2 generating essentially breakeven results (-$0.01 EPS) on $52.3M revenue, even a modest recovery to $53.5M cannot deliver the $0.05 EPS consensus implies without either a meaningful gross margin expansion or SG&A reduction—neither of which I see evidence of in recent disclosures.

The 66% surge in short interest to 5.9% of float in January validates my bearish view and suggests institutional investors share my skepticism about the company's profitability trajectory. Director Kenneth Halverson's recent stock sale, while routine, adds incremental negative sentiment. The Nxbeam partnership is strategically interesting for long-term RF & microwave positioning but contributes zero revenue in Q3 2026. My $53.5M revenue estimate assumes 2-3% sequential recovery from the Q2 destocking trough, gross margin of 30.7%, SG&A of $15.7M, and a -$200K non-operating headwind—generating operating income of ~$700K and net income of ~$440K, which translates to $0.03 EPS on 12.7M diluted shares.

To change my view, I would need to see evidence of SG&A discipline (sub-$15.5M), a revenue step-change above $55M, or meaningful gross margin expansion above 32%. The Nxbeam partnership and elevated short interest are key items to monitor, but neither alters my near-term earnings calculus. My confidence level is medium given the inherent unpredictability of non-operating income and the limited visibility into segment-level demand.

My Q3 2026 forecast for RGP maintains a near-breakeven $0.03 EPS on $106M revenue, unchanged from my February 17th estimate as no material new information has emerged in the past 24 hours. The core investment thesis remains intact: the January 2026 workforce reduction is creating a significant one-time SG&A reset that will produce the first near-breakeven quarter since Q1 2026. I project SG&A declining from $54.4M in Q2 to approximately $38M in Q3 as severance accruals reverse (~$10M benefit) and ongoing headcount savings materialize (~$5M benefit).

The key tension in this forecast is between cost savings (bullish) and revenue capacity constraints (bearish). The workforce reduction, while necessary for margin improvement, directly limits billable consultant hours and thus revenue generation. I'm modeling a 10% sequential revenue decline to $106M, which is more conservative than a simple seasonal pattern would suggest because the company has structurally reduced its ability to service demand. Gross margins should remain stable around 37% as the pay/bill ratio is unchanged - the company is essentially right-sizing its cost structure to a smaller revenue base.

My variant view versus the limited consensus ($0.04 EPS) is that the severance accrual reversal creates a one-time benefit that produces a near-breakeven quarter, but this is purely mechanical and not indicative of sustainable profitability. The 7.2% dividend yield highlighted in recent news is a warning sign, not a value signal - the company's earnings power has deteriorated significantly and the dividend may not be sustainable beyond FY2026. I would revise my estimate downward if management signals additional restructuring or if Q3 revenue guidance comes in below $105M.

My Q3 FY26 estimate of $0.36 EPS on $1.498B revenue maintains a modest 2.9% premium to Street's $0.35 EPS consensus while fundamentally diverging from the Street's $1.93B revenue figure. The critical insight driving my differentiated view is that the Street's revenue consensus appears completely misaligned with RPM's fiscal calendar and historical seasonal patterns. Q3 (February-April) has consistently been RPM's weakest quarter due to construction and DIY seasonality - Q3 FY25 revenue was $1.48B, and there's no fundamental catalyst supporting 30%+ sequential growth from Q2's $1.91B to reach $1.93B. I believe the Street consensus may be reflecting incorrect quarter alignment or data error.

My segment-level analysis shows Consumer Group facing continued headwinds from the housing market with mortgage rates above 7% suppressing both DIY activity and new home-related product demand. However, Construction Products Group should benefit modestly from Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) funding flowing into commercial and infrastructure projects, partially offsetting consumer weakness. The MAP 2025 margin improvement program continues to support gross margins around 38.3%, though Q3's lower revenue base creates natural operating deleverage. The Q2 FY26 EPS miss of -19.5% raises some questions about margin sustainability, but Q3 is structurally a lower-margin quarter anyway due to fixed cost deleverage.

What would change my view: If RPM announces a material acquisition that closed in Q3 adding significant revenue, the Street's higher revenue consensus could be correct. Additionally, if housing indicators show unexpected improvement in spring selling season data, Consumer Group could outperform my conservative -2% YoY estimate. The key swing factor remains whether the Street's $1.93B revenue figure reflects actual analyst models or a data aggregation error - I have high conviction the seasonal pattern supports my ~$1.5B revenue estimate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 forecast for Sugi Holdings maintains a ¥38 EPS estimate, representing a ¥1 discount to Wall Street's ¥39 consensus. This conservative stance reflects my concern about continued operating margin compression, which I project will reach approximately 4.0% in Q4, down from 4.2% in Q3 2026 and 5.7% in Q4 2025. The margin deterioration stems from persistent labor cost inflation in Japan's tight employment market combined with increased pharmacy service mix that carries structurally lower margins than traditional retail products.

The key differentiation in my analysis versus Street consensus centers on operating leverage dynamics. While analysts appear to assume margin stabilization, I observe a clear downward trend in operating income: ¥13.81B in Q4 2025 → ¥12.68B in Q2 2026 → ¥10.42B in Q3 2026. This trajectory suggests Q4 2026 operating income of approximately ¥9.8B on ¥246B revenue. The pharmacy segment tailwind (3-4% growth from aging demographics) is real but insufficient to offset the margin headwind. Same-store sales remain tepid at 1-2% amid broader Japanese consumer uncertainty.

My conviction remains low due to severe data quality issues in the available financial data. The Q1 2026 figures appear to be in USD rather than JPY, creating a discontinuity that undermines trend analysis. Until this anomaly is resolved, any forecast carries significant uncertainty. I would revise my view upward if operating margins stabilize above 4.2% or if same-store sales acceleration materializes beyond 2%. Conversely, evidence of accelerating margin compression or competitive share losses would push my estimate lower.

The Street appears overly pessimistic on SMPL's near-term earnings power for three reasons: (1) Q1's 32.3% gross margin was a trough driven by exceptional promotional activity that management indicated would moderate - historical patterns show Q2 margins typically improve 150-200bps off Q1; (2) Quest brand momentum (+7-8% YoY) is being underweighted while Atkins concerns are being overweighted - Quest now represents ~65% of revenues and its salty snacks expansion is driving genuine household penetration gains; (3) Share count reduction from the aggressive $99.6M Q1 buyback at 52-week lows creates meaningful EPS accretion that Street models lag in capturing.

This alone accounts for $0.02+ of my above-consensus call. The key pushback is whether margin recovery materializes - if promotional intensity persists and gross margins stay at 33% or below, my estimate would need to come down another $0.02-0.03. However, the combination of post-holiday promotional reset, Quest's pricing power in the better-for-you snacking category, and management's historical tendency to beat Q2 estimates by 5-10% supports my constructive stance.

I would revise my estimate lower if: (1) Channel checks indicate promotional intensity is actually increasing rather than moderating; (2) OWYN distribution losses expand beyond current assumptions; (3) Management signals on the Q1 call that margin headwinds are more persistent than temporary. The 'Bull Case' requires an immediate realization of AI efficiencies or a sudden spike in high-margin software/service attach rates, neither of which is visible in current channel data. My conviction is high that volume will surprise to the upside, but profitability will disappoint, leading to a 'hollow beat' that the market will punish.

The key swing factor is whether the Street's conservatism reflects actual demand weakness I'm missing or simply sentiment overcorrection to the leadership change headlines. My conviction remains medium given the transition uncertainty, but the mechanical EPS accretion from buybacks provides a quantifiable floor that the consensus appears to ignore.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 represents a 6.9% premium to Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven by three key factors the market appears to be underweighting. First, the mechanical EPS accretion from Seven & i's aggressive share repurchase program is being underappreciated - the share count has declined from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 (a 6% reduction in three quarters), and I project further reduction to 2.18B by Q4 FY26 based on continued buyback pace of ~¥89B quarterly. This share count reduction alone provides 12% EPS tailwind year-over-year. Second, Q4 seasonal strength should drive operating margin expansion to 5.6% vs the trailing four-quarter average of 4.4%, reflecting convenience store mix shift and cost rationalization benefits. Third, the CVS Health Q4 results showing steady retail execution with $400B+ 2026 revenue guidance provides supportive read-through for 7-Eleven North American operations.

The key risk to my thesis is gross margin normalization from Q3's anomalous 29.1% level. I'm modeling 26% for Q4, which reflects partial normalization but still above the 19-20% levels seen in Q1-Q2 FY26. If Q3's elevated margin was purely one-time inventory gains or accounting adjustments that fully reverse, gross margin could fall to 24%, reducing my EPS estimate by ~¥4.50. Additionally, if the Couche-Tard acquisition discussions intensify, management may preserve cash optionality by slowing the buyback pace, which would increase share count and reduce EPS. I would revise my estimate downward if I see evidence of buyback deceleration in company announcements or if consumer data out of Japan shows meaningful weakness in convenience store traffic.

Maintaining my prior estimates as no material new information has emerged since my last forecast. The news flow remains supportive with no negative Seven & i specific developments, and the broader S&P 500 earnings strength (96 of 123 companies posting EPS growth) suggests a healthy consumer environment globally.

My Q4 2026 EPS forecast of ¥38.0 represents a fundamental rejection of the Wall Street consensus figure of $0.19, which is clearly erroneous due to a currency/data provider error. The historical EPS data unmistakably demonstrates quarterly earnings consistently in the ¥19-42 range (Q4 2025: ¥42.14, Q3 2026: ¥33.0, Q2 2026: ¥29.0, Q1 2026: ¥19.0), making a $0.19 consensus mathematically impossible for a company generating ¥70-110B in quarterly net income. My estimate reflects a sequential improvement from Q3's ¥33.0 driven by Q4 seasonal strength, while remaining below last year's ¥42.14 due to ongoing margin pressure from supermarket restructuring and modestly weaker yen translation effects.

The key drivers supporting my ¥38.0 estimate include: (1) Revenue of ¥2.48T reflecting Q4 seasonal strength in convenience store operations with 2-3% SSS growth in Japan and stable North American operations; (2) Gross margin sustained at ~29% as cost discipline holds; (3) Continued aggressive share buybacks reducing diluted shares to ~2.35B from 2.44B in Q3, providing meaningful EPS accretion of approximately ¥1.5-2.0; (4) Operating income around ¥120B consistent with recent quarterly run-rate. The ¥38.0 estimate implies net income of approximately ¥89B, which is within the historical range and reflects the normalized earnings power of the business.

Key risks that could prove my thesis wrong include: (1) Unexpected deterioration in Japan consumer spending, though recent sector data remains supportive; (2) Couche-Tard M&A resolution creating one-time charges or strategic uncertainty; (3) FX volatility beyond my ¥155/USD assumption; (4) Slower-than-expected progress on supermarket segment restructuring. I maintain medium conviction given the stable operational trends but acknowledge uncertainty around capital allocation and M&A dynamics.

My modeling assumes a 70% effective tax rate - meaningfully below Q1's 111% - which could prove conservative if deferred tax timing issues persist.

The Feb 19 virtual roadshow (tomorrow) is the key near-term catalyst - if management provides clarity on tax normalization or structural changes to the tax regime, I would reassess. Absent that, I maintain low conviction due to the inherent unpredictability of Tanzania's mining tax treatment, but believe my estimate is more realistic than the Street's implicit assumption of developed-market tax rates in an emerging market mining jurisdiction.

My revenue estimate of ¥148.5T assumes 10% QoQ growth on seasonal strength but still reflects more conservative segment assumptions than consensus.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of China demand inflection in AC drives/servos from channel checks or peer commentary; (2) Inventory levels declining below ¥210B indicating successful destocking; (3) Gross margin recovery above 35% demonstrating pricing power intact. Without these signals, I see the Street's ¥46.39 EPS as over-optimistic and maintain my conservative stance with medium conviction given data quality and visibility constraints.

I continue to treat the cached consensus EPS ($46.39) as likely non-comparable to the cached revenue consensus (~$0.88B) given the supplied historical dataset’s clear unit/currency inconsistencies (e.g., quarters showing ~$0.91B revenue alongside much larger profit figures). The only internally coherent anchor in the provided history is the ~$0.9B revenue quarter (2025-08-31: revenue ~$0.91B with EPS ~$0.30), so I forecast Q4 2026 on that normalized scale.

Against that normalized baseline, my variant view is that Q4 2026 is a stabilization quarter: revenue modestly above consensus at ~$0.90B (vs $0.88B) with Motion Control steady and Robotics no longer deteriorating but not rebounding. Margins improve slightly on mix/cost normalization while SG&A remains controlled, producing EPS of ~$0.26.

I would change my mind if (1) evidence emerges of a true Robotics demand inflection (orders/shipment acceleration) that would lift revenue and operating leverage materially, or (2) channel/order data indicate renewed pushouts that would pull revenue below ~$0.86B and pressure margins. The largest risk remains the data-scale mismatch, which can cause headline EPS to print in a different unit than this normalized model.

risks: Order pushouts/cancellations in China/semicap segments could cut revenue by ~3–6%
Pricing pressure in Robotics could compress gross margin by ~100–200 bps
Model risk from unit/currency inconsistencies in provided historical dataset (EPS/revenue scale mismatch)
margin_factors: Gross margin slightly improves on mix and easing input-cost pressure vs prior normalized quarter
OpEx disciplined with limited operating leverage; SG&A held near normalized run-rate
Net interest slightly positive; non-operating assumed small net tailwind
revenue_drivers: Robotics: modest sequential stabilization; no sharp rebound assumed (small positive vs consensus)
Motion Control: steady baseline demand supports flattish-to-slightly-up revenue
FX/translation & reporting-unit noise: limited use in model; primary forecast anchored to ~$0.9B quarterly scale

Granular data shows Q3 +7% QoQ beat, inventory build for Q4 peak, no weak signals; Street conflicts lead to lowball to avoid upside surprise risk. Would change mind on direct Yaskawa pre-announce cut or peer guidance walks; otherwise high conviction beat.
